extracted.intended_audience: readers of political philosophy and general readers interested in law, liberty, and the role of government
extracted.subtask_description: A book preface / political essay arguing a classical-liberal view of law and government: defines law as organised force limited to preventing injustice, defends broad individual liberty, and criticises legislators, social engineers, and state social planning. Contains normative standards about the proper domain and limits of law and the dangers of legislative omnipotence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law is common force organised to prevent injustice (Law is Justice)
rubrics_metrics.description: “Law is common force organised to prevent injustice;--in short, Law is Justice.” — The law's rightful mission is to secure persons and property from injury and to organise individual right of legitimate defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly insists that the law's domain is the domain of force (justice) and not broader moral or philanthropic ends. Law can only legitimately use collective force for lawful defence and to prevent rights of one from interfering with another. Any use of law beyond this (to regulate conscience, education, sentiments, exchanges, etc.) is beyond its lawful domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of law — do not regulate conscience, ideas, education, sentiments, or private enjoyments
rubrics_metrics.description: The mission of the law is not to regulate our consciences, ideas, will, education, sentiments, works, exchanges, gifts, or enjoyments; its mission is to prevent the rights of one from interfering with those of another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law departs from this limited role and becomes philanthropic, religious, literary, or artistic, it enters vagueness and uncertainty and becomes a battleground for competing Utopias. The author warns that leaving the law this latitude invites endless complaints and revolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberty as the union of all liberties (definition of liberty)
rubrics_metrics.description: Liberty is described as "the union of all liberties, the liberty of conscience, of instruction, of association, of the press, of locomotion, of labour, and of exchange" — i.e., the free exercise, for all, of all the inoffensive faculties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception implies the destruction of all despotisms (even legal despotism) and reduction of law to its rational sphere: to regulate legitimate defence and repress injustice. Liberty entails that individuals have access to instruction and instruments of labour so as to exercise their faculties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject legislative omnipotence and the infallibility of the legislator
rubrics_metrics.description: The text criticises the notion that the legislator is omnipotent or infallible and that society should be moulded by great men: ‘the omnipotence of the law,’ ‘the infallibility of the legislator,’ and the view that ‘men are nothing but raw material’ to be made by legislators are condemned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislators are part of the human race and liable to error and interest; they must not presume the right to impose social plans by law. The author challenges organisers to prove their supposed superiority rather than assume the right to govern by fiat.

rubrics_metrics.name: Oppose social engineering by the State (do not impose utopias through law)
rubrics_metrics.description: State-driven imposition of social projects — e.g., providing instruments of labour, gratuitous credit, universal instruction, or fixed standards of wellbeing — is criticised as converting law into the instrument for enforcing a chosen Utopia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues organisers may invent and propagate plans, but they have no right to subject others to them by force or taxation. Making such social programmes legal obligations invites conflict between competing schemes and endless litigation/complaint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Against dictatorship and the use of terror to enforce virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: The author reproves doctrines that defend extraordinary magistracies and terror to impose moral regeneration (quoting Mably and Robespierre: 'the means to be adopted, during its establishment, is terror').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dictatorships and terror are condemned as illegitimate means to impose morality; moral reform should not be effectuated by extraordinary magistracies with considerable power or by terror. The imagination of the people may be 'impressed' by such measures, but this is rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Government responsibility and scope cause revolutionary risk
rubrics_metrics.description: When government undertakes to regulate wages, provide asylum, grant gratuitous credit, or otherwise assume responsibility for social welfare, its failures become the sole grounds for popular blame and revolution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extending the dominion of law (and thereby government responsibility) increases the probability of revolutions because every disappointment in the state's assumed duties will be attributed to it. Therefore the law's scope should be limited to reduce such systemic risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer minimal interference by law for greater wellbeing
rubrics_metrics.description: Nations are happiest and most moral where the law interferes least with private activity; where government is least felt; where individuality has most scope and public opinion most influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical appeal: lighter, less complicated administration, lighter and less unequal taxation, and fewer fetters on transactions, meetings, and associations lead to more peaceful, moral, and prosperous societies according to the author.

rubrics_metrics.name: People possess initiative; do not presume mankind passive and to be improved only by legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: The author rejects the view (prominent in some 17th–18th-century writers and some socialists) that mankind is 'raw material' or radically passive and must be formed entirely by a legislator; instead people have initiative and perfectibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow social organs and individual faculties to develop through exercise, experience, and liberty (analogy of traveller with savage tribe's quacks). The author supports trial of liberty rather than artificial social prescriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law cannot be philanthropic or equalising without losing fixed limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Justice is described as a 'given quantity, immutable and unchangeable' while philanthropy and fraternity have no fixed limits; making law philanthropic leads to vagueness and endless extension of state power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If law becomes the instrument for fraternity it must answer competing visions (e.g., favour producers, favour workers, provide luxury everywhere) and will become the battlefield for everyone's dreams. The author counsels against such expansion.

rubrics_metrics.name: The legislator's proper function: secure pre-existing persons and property, not create rights
rubrics_metrics.description: It is not true that the legislator has absolute power over persons and property, since they pre-exist; his work is only to secure them from injury. Law organises individual rights that existed before legitimate defence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Law's role is protective, not creative. Using law to 'dispose of the consumers in favour of the producers' or to impose industrial or moral programmes exceeds the legislator's proper function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject state monopolies, centralization, and artificial interventions (tariffs, universitary monopoly, monopolising banks, social workshops)
rubrics_metrics.description: The author enumerates a catalogue of state interventions to be rejected: 'social workshops, governmental whims, centralization, tariffs, universities, State religions, gratuitous or monopolising banks, limitations, restrictions, moralisations, and equalisation by taxation.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These artificial methods are grouped as 'rings, chains, hooks, and pincers' that impede the natural development of society. The recommendation is to 'reject all systems, and make trial of liberty.'
